n: In this lecture we will examine gaseous poisons, that is, methane and carbon monoxide, from the forensic chemical point of view. The plan has three parts: methane poisoning, carbon monoxide poisoning, and the analysis of carboxyhaemoglobin in blood by chemical and physicochemical methods. Key words and concepts: carbon monoxide, carboxyhaemoglobin, chemical and physicochemical methods. The aim is to introduce the significance of carbon monoxide in forensic chemical practice, the compounds it forms with haemoglobin, and their properties.

We begin with methane. Methane is a natural gas, colourless and odourless. Because it has no smell, it is hard to notice. Methane poisoning occurs in mines, at vehicle gas filling stations, and also in homes as a result of improper use of natural gas. Remember: besides methane, natural gas also contains propane and butane.

Now, the specimen and storage conditions for analysing methane. In analysing these gases, it is appropriate to use the lungs and brain as the biological specimen. It has been established that these gases are preserved in biomaterial for no less than three weeks from the time the poison entered the body, and in the brain and lungs for up to 4 weeks. Therefore the biomaterial must be stored in hermetically sealed containers, otherwise the gas may be lost.

The identity and amount of methane are determined mainly by gas-liquid chromatography, GLC for short. The procedure is as follows. 500 µl of blood and 500 mg of minced biomaterial are placed in a penicillin vial and closed with a rubber stopper. Then the vial is heated for 10 minutes in a boiling water bath. After heating, the vapour-gas phase is withdrawn from the vial with a syringe and analysed by GLC. Such an analysis is called headspace analysis.

Now, the GLC conditions. The detector is a flame ionisation detector, the carrier gas is nitrogen at a rate of 30 ml/min. The column thermostat operates at 50°C and the vaporiser at 150°C. The column is Polysorb-1, of size 100 x 3 mm. Methane is identified by its absolute retention time. Under the stated conditions the retention time of methane is 3 minutes. That is, the peak that emerges on the chromatogram at this time is considered to belong to methane.

Now we turn to carbon monoxide. Carbon(II) oxide, that is, carbon monoxide, is a colourless, odourless, tasteless, fast-acting toxic substance. It is very poorly soluble in water and burns with a blue flame: 2CO + O2 gives 2CO2. Importantly, a mixture of carbon monoxide with air at 16 to 73% can explode. So this gas is not only toxic but also explosive in a certain ratio.

How is carbon monoxide formed? It appears when organic substances, coal, gas and other fuels burn incompletely. The causes of poisoning vary. In industry: faulty operation of blast furnaces; at home: closing the stove damper before the fire has burned out, and putting coal in a sandal. On the streets, poisoning occurs from carbon monoxide in exhaust gases due to a vehicle fault. The literature also describes many cases of suicide and homicide with carbon monoxide.

Let us consider other sources of carbon monoxide. Natural gas fuel may contain 4-30% carbon monoxide, depending on the type of gas. In "water gas", obtained by passing steam over red-hot coal, carbon monoxide makes up 40-50%: C + H2O gives CO + H2. When artillery shells are fired or a mine explodes, about 30% carbon monoxide is formed as a result of the explosion. The table shows the CO content in the three sources.

We turn to the clinical signs of poisoning. Because carbon monoxide has no smell, poisoning with it occurs quickly and suddenly. First a severe headache, weakness, nausea and vomiting, ringing in the ears and strong palpitations appear. Then the jaws clench, and from lack of oxygen the person loses consciousness. Cardiac activity and respiration weaken, which leads to death.

On examining the deceased, the following picture is observed. Cadaveric lividity is bright red. Because of carboxyhaemoglobin the blood becomes bright red, and the liver, kidneys and lungs are reddened. Signs of haemorrhage are observed in the brain tissue. These signs indicate carbon monoxide poisoning.

Now, the main mechanism of poisoning. CO combines very readily with haemoglobin to form stable carboxyhaemoglobin: HbO2 + CO gives HbCO + O2. As a result, haemoglobin loses its ability to carry oxygen, and the victim dies of oxygen deficiency. Do not forget: if carboxyhaemoglobin is found in the blood, this proves that the victim was poisoned with carbon monoxide.

We compare the affinity of carbon monoxide and oxygen for haemoglobin. The rate at which carbon monoxide combines with haemoglobin is 300 times greater than that of oxygen. Dissociation is the reverse: the release of CO from HbCO is 3600 times slower than the release of O2 from oxyhaemoglobin. As a result, haemoglobin loses its ability to carry oxygen. This means that once carbon monoxide has bound, it is very hard to displace it from haemoglobin.

t: Carboxyhaemoglobin level and degree of poisoning
n: The carboxyhaemoglobin level determines the degree of poisoning. If carboxyhaemoglobin in the blood is 20-30%, the poisoning is mild. At 30-35% it is moderate, at 35-50% severe. At 50-60% strong poisoning is observed, with convulsions and loss of consciousness. When it reaches 70-80%, death occurs. The table compares the COHb level and the degree.

Let us recall the forms of haemoglobin in blood. In the blood of a person poisoned with carbon monoxide there may be deoxyhaemoglobin Hb, oxyhaemoglobin OHb, carboxyhaemoglobin COHb and, in part, methaemoglobin MtHb. Remember: methaemoglobin does not combine with carbon monoxide. In muscle tissue there are myoglobin forms: deoxymyoglobin MHb, oxymyoglobin OMHb and carboxymyoglobin COMHb.

t: Persistence and elimination of carbon monoxide
n: On the persistence and elimination of carbon monoxide in the body. Carbon monoxide is eliminated from the body only through the respiratory tract. There is an opinion that it persists in the body for a long time, up to 122 days. According to another opinion, it can no longer be detected after 25-40 hours. As for air: a content of 0.07-0.08% carbon monoxide in the air of homes and workplaces is dangerous to life, while the permissible concentration in air is 0.02 mg/l.

We turn to the methods of detecting carbon monoxide. Detection is based on finding carboxyhaemoglobin in the blood by chemical and physicochemical methods. Physicochemical methods include spectroscopic, spectrophotometric, photometric and gas chromatographic methods. To detect it in a specimen, the specimen is minced, the blood is separated and the composition of the blood is examined. To detect carbon monoxide in air, the air is passed through animal blood, the gas is collected in the blood, and this blood is analysed.

t: Sampling: from the specimen and from air
n: We compare two ways of sampling. To detect carbon monoxide in a biological specimen, the specimen is minced, the blood is separated, and then the composition of the blood is examined. In detecting carbon monoxide in air, by contrast, the air is passed through animal blood, and the gas is collected in the blood. Then the blood through which the air was passed is itself analysed. That is, in the first case the blood is separated from the specimen, and in the second the blood serves as the means of collecting the air.

The spectroscopic method. In the spectroscope, Fraunhofer lines are visible in the D and E region of the spectrum. Oxyhaemoglobin gives two absorption bands between the D and E regions: 577-589 and 536-556 nm. Carboxyhaemoglobin forms a spectrum in the regions 564-579 and 523-536 nm. Reduced haemoglobin gives a broad band at 543-596 nm. By these differences we distinguish the compounds from each other.

In spectroscopy, a test with ammonium sulphide is performed. Under the action of the reducing agent, that is, ammonium sulphide, the two bands of oxyhaemoglobin merge to form a broad band between 543 and 596 nm. If carboxyhaemoglobin is present in the blood, the spectra in this region remain unchanged. The reason is that carboxyhaemoglobin is not reduced to haemoglobin by ammonium sulphide. In this way poisoned blood can be distinguished from ordinary blood.

The principle of the spectrophotometric method is as follows. The method is based on reducing oxy- and carboxyhaemoglobin to deoxyhaemoglobin and determining the absorbance. Identity and amount are determined from the absorption spectra in the region 450-620 nm. For this, three solutions are prepared: A, the blood under test; B, a mixture of carboxyhaemoglobin and deoxyhaemoglobin, that is, solution A with sodium dithionite added; V, carboxyhaemoglobin only, that is, blood saturated with CO.

t: Solutions A, B and V: comparison
n: We compare solutions A, B and V. Solution A is the blood under test; 1 ml of blood is diluted with buffer or 0.1% NH3 to 100 ml. Solution B is solution A with 3-4 mg of Na2S2O4·2H2O added; it contains carboxyhaemoglobin and deoxyhaemoglobin. Solution V is solution A saturated with CO, with 5-7 mg of dithionite added; it contains only carboxyhaemoglobin. All three solutions must be clear. The light absorption spectrum of solutions B and V is measured in the region 450-620 nm, and both spectra are plotted on one graph.

The procedure for preparing solutions A and B. For solution A, phosphate buffer pH = 7.38 or 0.1% aqueous ammonia solution is added to 1 ml of blood without sediment to make 100 ml. The solution must be clear. For solution B, solution A is placed in the spectrophotometer cuvette and 3-4 mg of sodium dithionite, that is, Na2S2O4·2H2O, is added. In this, oxyhaemoglobin is completely reduced to deoxyhaemoglobin. The clarity of the solution is again checked.

What is the role of sodium dithionite? Sodium dithionite, that is, hydrosulphite, completely reduces oxyhaemoglobin to deoxyhaemoglobin. In preparing solution B, solution A in the spectrophotometer cuvette is treated with 3-4 mg of Na2S2O4·2H2O. After the reagent is added, the clarity of the solution is checked. In solution V, 5-7 mg of dithionite is added to convert methaemoglobin into deoxyhaemoglobin.

t: Reducing agents: ammonium sulphide and dithionite
n: We compare two reducing agents. Ammonium sulphide is used in the spectroscopic method. Under its action the oxyhaemoglobin bands merge and form a broadened band at 543-596 nm, while the carboxyhaemoglobin spectrum does not change. Sodium dithionite is used in the spectrophotometric method and completely reduces oxyhaemoglobin to deoxyhaemoglobin. In solution B its amount is 3-4 mg, in solution V 5-7 mg. Remember: carboxyhaemoglobin is not reduced to haemoglobin by ammonium sulphide.

t: Preparing solution V: saturation with CO
n: To prepare solution V, the blood is saturated with carbon monoxide. Carbon monoxide is generated from concentrated H2SO4 and formic acid. A 10% alkali solution retains the formic acid vapour, then the gas is passed through water. The purified gas is led into the vessel with solution A, where oxyhaemoglobin is completely converted into carboxyhaemoglobin. To convert methaemoglobin into deoxyhaemoglobin, 5-7 mg of sodium dithionite is added to the vessel, and it is saturated with carbon monoxide again. The solution must be clear.

Spectral maxima and isosbestic points. Deoxyhaemoglobin, that is, solution B, gives a single spectral maximum at 557 nm. Carboxyhaemoglobin gives two maxima at 541 and 571 nm. The two spectra intersect at 550, 565 and 580 nm. These points are called isosbestic points.

t: Spectral points: maxima and isosbestic points
n: We summarise the spectral points. The spectrum is measured in the region 450-620 nm. The haemoglobin maximum is at 557 nm, the carboxyhaemoglobin maxima at 541 and 571 nm. The carboxyhaemoglobin and deoxyhaemoglobin curves intersect at 550, 565 and 580 nm; these are isosbestic points. The D2 value is measured at 550 nm, at the point where the curves intersect. D1 for carboxyhaemoglobin is measured at 538 nm. This graph is used to determine the amount.

Absorbance is measured at two wavelengths. Carboxyhaemoglobin is measured at a wavelength of 538 nm; this is D1. At precisely this wavelength, the difference between the absorbances of carboxyhaemoglobin and deoxyhaemoglobin has its greatest value. The second measurement is made at the isosbestic point, that is, at 550 nm; this is D2. As the reference solution, 0.1% ammonia or buffer is used.

The ammonia variant of the procedure. In determining the amount of carboxyhaemoglobin, an ammonia solution may be used instead of buffer. The blood is placed in a 100 ml volumetric flask, made up to the mark with 0.1% aqueous ammonia solution, mixed and poured into a 1 cm cuvette. Crystals of sodium hydrosulphite are added to the solution and it is shaken. Then the absorbance is measured at 538 nm and at the isosbestic point. The reference solution is 0.1% ammonia.

We compare the buffer and ammonia variants. In the buffer variant, 1 ml of blood is diluted with phosphate buffer pH = 7.38 to 100 ml, and solutions A, B and V are prepared. In the ammonia variant, the blood is diluted with 0.1% aqueous ammonia solution to 100 ml, the solution is poured into a 1 cm cuvette, and crystals of sodium hydrosulphite are added directly and the solution is shaken. The reference solution is 0.1% ammonia in the ammonia variant; in the buffer variant, buffer or water.

Now, calculating the percentage of carboxyhaemoglobin. DCOHb is the absorbance at 538 nm of solution V additionally saturated with CO. DHbCOHb is the absorbance of solution B at 538 nm after dithionite. DHbi is the absorbance of solution B at the isosbestic point, with coefficient K = 0.372. The calculation formula: P = 100 - [(DV - DB)·100] / (Dizob · K). Here DV and DB are the absorbances of solutions V and B at 538 nm, and Dizob is that at the isosbestic point.

Now, the general principle of chemical methods. Chemical methods are based on the fact that carboxyhaemoglobin is a more stable substance than oxyhaemoglobin. If unpoisoned blood is diluted with water, a brown colour forms, whereas blood with carboxyhaemoglobin does not change its bright red colour. If caustic alkali is added to normal blood, a bluish-black liquid forms, whereas blood poisoned with carbon monoxide keeps its colour.

t: Chemical methods: tannin, yellow prussiate, lead
n: Three more chemical tests. Normal blood forms a grey substance with tannin, whereas blood with carboxyhaemoglobin does not change colour. Yellow prussiate of potash and acetic acid give a brown colour in normal blood, with no change in poisoned blood. Lead acetate stains normal blood a dirty blue, whereas blood with carboxyhaemoglobin keeps its colour. The table gives the reaction of normal blood to each reagent.

t: Chemical methods: formalin and copper sulphate
n: The chemical tests continue. Formalin forms a dirty brown substance with normal blood, but with blood containing carboxyhaemoglobin there is no change at all. With copper sulphate solution, pure blood turns green, while blood poisoned with carbon monoxide does not change its bright red colour. In the Hoppe-Seyler test, 1 ml of 30% NaOH is added to 0.5 ml of blood, and it is left for 1 minute. Blood with carboxyhaemoglobin keeps a bright red colour; it is compared with normal blood.

t: Chemical tests: normal blood and blood with COHb
n: We summarise the chemical tests by table. These methods are based on the fact that carboxyhaemoglobin is more stable than oxyhaemoglobin. Normal blood changes colour under the action of water, alkali, tannin, formalin and copper sulphate, whereas blood with carboxyhaemoglobin does not. Yellow prussiate of potash and acetic acid give a brown colour in normal blood, and lead acetate gives a dirty blue. In the table, normal blood and COHb blood are given side by side.

Microdiffusion and the PdCl2 method. 1 ml of blood is placed in the chamber and 1 ml of 10% H2SO4 is added. 2 ml of a 0.1% PdCl2 solution is placed in the inner chamber. The chamber is left for 1 hour. The following reaction takes place: CO + PdCl2 + H2O gives 2HCl + CO2 + Pd. Metallic Pd forms a grey film. This method makes it possible to detect CO in blood by microdiffusion.

Evaluating the result. When the carboxyhaemoglobin level reaches 70-80%, death occurs. These cases depend on the environment and on the person's body. In the quantitative method, an error of ±3% is permitted when COHb is from 3 to 20%, and ±5% when it is above 20%. So, in evaluating the result, the permitted error must be taken into account.

We conclude the lecture. Methane is determined by GLC, that is, with the help of headspace analysis; the specimen is lung and brain. Carbon monoxide forms stable carboxyhaemoglobin with haemoglobin; the substance determined is COHb. Methods: chemical tests, spectroscopy and spectrophotometry, using solutions A, B and V, 538 nm and K = 0.372. For self-check, test yourself on: COHb levels, isosbestic points, the role of dithionite, and revise the chemical tests.
